rv.q: Cow | Deer is a daring, wordless evocation of the perils and pleasures of animal life.
And the calf’s birth could be the most captivating stage scene of the year.
It’s hypotonic, like a dance - I became utterly engrossed in the dizzying technical rhythms of the Mitchell-directed performance.
For all its ecological pretensions, this oddball production ends up leaving you longing for a little old-fashioned silence.
This captivating hour-long experiment lets the spectator have full agency when it comes to its interpretation.

If an audience can tune into the details, then there is much to gain from this impressive co-production, where deep listening and imagination are recommended to connect to the narrative and engage in a remarkable world of inventive possibility.
It is fascinating to see the concentration with which performers turn fists to hooves.
I have to say that the effect of the performance is both mind-expandingly extraordinary and brain-crushingly banal.
Mitchell’s message, buried under the moos, snorts, and cud-chewing, remains stubbornly unclear.
Mitchell has always pushed the boundaries of what theatre can be since The Waves in 2006, but Cow |Deer sees her chewing the cud with limited results.
But while all these achievements fairly deserve acknowledgment, the piece still remains closer to a well-executed germinal idea than a fully developed show.
This won't be for all theatregoers.
